::: {.resource-intro}
**The essential idea:** A reference manager such as Zotero stores
bibliographic records and links them to PDFs, notes, and drafts. It
saves time and reduces errors, but it does not replace careful reading
or checking that your citations are accurate.
:::

## Why use a reference manager?

A reference manager is a personal database of your sources. It helps
you:

- **Capture** citation information from databases, library catalogs,
  publisher pages, and DOIs with one click.
- **Organize** sources by project, theme, or reading status.
- **Connect** each source to its PDF, your notes, and your annotations.
- **Cite** sources in your word processor and build a bibliography in
  any citation style.
- **Reuse** sources across courses and projects for years.

Common options include [Zotero](https://www.zotero.org/) (free and open
source), Mendeley, and EndNote. Your library may support one in
particular and offer workshops. This page uses Zotero for its
examples, but the practices apply to any of these tools.

**Why accuracy matters:** Citation errors are surprisingly common, even
in published research. A review of studies in medical journals
estimated that about 14.5% of cited claims were quoted incorrectly, and
most of those errors were major: the cited source failed to support,
was unrelated to, or contradicted the claim (Mogull, 2017). A reference
manager can make your citations *formatted* correctly. Only you can
make sure they're *accurate*.

## Core practices

### 1. Capture the record

- **Save from the source.** Use the browser connector (e.g., Zotero
  Connector) on a database or publisher page, or add by identifier
  (DOI, ISBN, PubMed ID).
- **Check the metadata immediately.** Automatic capture often gets
  details wrong. Check:
  - **Authors:** spelling, order, and initials; organizations as
    authors
  - **Title:** capitalization, and subtitles that are missing or
    duplicated
  - **Publication:** full journal name, volume, issue, pages
  - **Date:** publication date, not access date
  - **Item type:** journal article, book, chapter, report, dataset,
    webpage
  - **Identifier:** DOI or stable URL
- **Attach or link the full text** where your access permits.
- **Add a quick note** on why the source matters to your project.

### 2. Organize for retrieval

- **Collections (folders)** for projects or courses. One item can live
  in several collections without being duplicated.
- **Tags** for themes, methods, or status. Keep a small, consistent
  set and write it down so you use it the same way every time.

| Tag type | Examples |
|---|---|
| Status | `to-read`, `read`, `cited`, `excluded` |
| Theme | `sediment`, `restoration`, `policy` |
| Method | `field-study`, `model`, `review`, `survey` |
| Screening | `include`, `exclude-scope`, `maybe` |

The screening tags match the log in [Reproducible Literature
Searching](literature-search.qmd).

- **Use duplicate detection** regularly, especially after importing
  from several databases.
- **Name attached files consistently** (e.g., `Author_Year_ShortTitle.pdf`).
  Zotero can rename attachments automatically.

### 3. Connect sources to notes

- **Annotate PDFs** inside the reference manager so your highlights and
  comments stay with the source. Zotero's built-in reader can pull
  annotations into a note with citations attached.
- **Write a short summary note** for each important source: research
  question, methods, key findings, limitations, and relevance. Use the
  same headings as your [synthesis matrix](literature-synthesis.qmd).
- **Keep quotations, paraphrases, and your own ideas visibly separate**
  in notes, with page numbers for anything quoted or paraphrased (see
  [Note Taking Methods](note-taking.qmd)).

### 4. Cite carefully

- **Install the word-processor plugin** (Word, Google Docs, or
  LibreOffice) and insert citations with it rather than typing them.
  The bibliography then updates automatically.
- **Choose the required style** (APA, MLA, Chicago, CSE, or a journal
  style), and check one or two entries against the official style
  guide.
- **Add page numbers** for direct quotations and specific claims.
- **Verify before submitting:**
  - Every in-text citation has a reference entry, and every reference
    is cited.
  - Each citation supports the specific claim it's attached to.
  - Capitalization and italics follow the style.
  - Nothing comes from an AI-generated reference you haven't checked
    against the original source (see [Ethical Research, Writing, and AI
    Use](research-ethics.qmd)).

### 5. Watch for retracted sources

Papers are sometimes retracted after publication because of errors or
misconduct. Zotero checks your library against the Retraction Watch
database, flags retracted items, and warns you when you try to cite
one (Zotero, 2019). This check currently works only for items with a
DOI or PubMed ID, which is another reason to make sure your records
include identifiers.

### 6. Back up and sync

- **Sync** your library to an account so it is backed up and available
  on other devices. Free storage for attached files is limited, so
  check your plan or your institution's options.
- **Export your library** periodically (e.g., as a `.bib` or `.ris`
  file) as an extra backup.
- **Don't keep your only copy of a library in a temporary location**
  such as a lab computer or a course drive that will be deleted.

### 7. Collaborate with group libraries

- **Use a shared group** for team projects, with an agreed set of
  collections and tags.
- **Keep interpretations separate:** Put shared, approved references in
  the group library, and keep personal notes and interpretations in
  your own library or in clearly labeled notes. This avoids mixing
  different people's conclusions.
- **Respect copyright and licensing** when sharing PDFs. Many licenses
  allow personal use only. Share citations or DOIs instead of files
  when in doubt.

## A simple workflow

1. Install a reference manager and its browser connector and
   word-processor plugin.
2. Create a collection for your project.
3. Import one source from a scholarly database and another by DOI.
4. Inspect and correct both metadata records.
5. Attach or link the full text where permitted.
6. Add a tag and a short note on why each source matters.
7. Insert both citations into a document with the plugin, then
   generate a bibliography in your required style.
8. Check the output against the style guide and the original sources.

## In context

::: {.callout-example}
A collaborative coastal monitoring project uses one shared collection
for approved references and personal notes for interpretation. This
reduces duplicate downloads without mixing different researchers'
conclusions. Before a report goes out, one team member checks that each
in-text citation supports its claim.
:::

::: {.callout-example}
A student writing a sociology paper imports twelve sources from two
databases. Duplicate detection merges three repeated records. While
checking metadata, the student finds a book chapter saved as a journal
article and a missing second author, and fixes both before citing.
:::

## Common pitfalls

- **Trusting automatic metadata.** Always check author names, titles,
  and item types.
- **Citing from memory or from abstracts.** Cite what you've actually
  read, and check that the source says what you claim.
- **Secondary citation by accident:** citing an original study you only
  know about through another paper. Either read the original, or cite
  it as a secondary source according to your style guide.
- **Tag sprawl:** dozens of near-duplicate tags (`restoration`,
  `Restoration`, `restor.`). Keep a short list.
- **Editing the bibliography by hand.** Manual edits are lost when the
  plugin refreshes. Fix the record in the library instead.

## Keep in mind

Back up or sync your library, and respect copyright and access
conditions when sharing PDFs. A reference manager is a tool for
accuracy, not a guarantee of it. You are responsible for every citation
in your work.
